answers: Cruz Riojas came from a troubled home: He was reportedly beaten by his stepfather, lived in a decrepit one-room lean-to with six other family members, and wore the same clothes to school every day, according to the Lubbock Avalanche-Journal. He also caused trouble in school and was known as a “holy terror,” says Linda Hooper, a teacher who first encountered Cruz in the early ‘80s, when he was 12 years old. But then an amazing thing happened: He started spending more time with Hooper, who would give him tasks to do around the classroom. He eventually began coming for visits at her home, where she lived with her husband and four daughters, often running the nearly eight miles between their two houses to get away from his stepfather. After an incident with his stepfather in 1983, Cruz’s mother asked if he could stay with the Hoopers for a few days till everything blew over. "He never left" after that, Hooper says. "I had him from then on." He became a part of the Hooper family, taking on a paper route to make money and doing better in school, placing out of special education classes by the time he graduated. More than a decade later, he was still part of the Hooper family—but he wanted to make it official by asking the Hoopers to adopt him right before his 30th birthday. “He said he wanted to honor us, and it was a big honor," Hooper tells Today. "I’ve always known he loved me, but this really showed he loved us.” The adoption went through in 1998, but Cruz "was my son from the day I kept him,” Hooper says. The family is just now telling their story for the first time. **Summary of News Passages**

In 1981, Linda Hooper, a veteran elementary school teacher in Lubbock, Texas, encountered a student named Cruz Riojas, who was known for his frequent and violent outbursts. Initially, Hooper found it difficult to accept him, calling him a "holy terror" and even threatening to quit if he were placed in her class. Cruz, who was two grade levels behind in reading and classified as a special education student, had a troubled home life, living in squalor with his mother and abusive stepfather. He often wore the same clothes to school and was plagued by lice, reflecting the poor conditions of his household.

Despite the challenges, Hooper began to see a change in Cruz during his sixth-grade year. He started helping in her classroom, and she began to treat him with kindness and patience. This led to a growing bond between them, and Cruz began spending more time at Hooper’s home, where he was given a new wardrobe, a job, and a sense of stability. His stepfather eventually kicked him out after a violent confrontation, and Cruz was temporarily placed with Hooper and her husband, Gale, a retired firefighter.

Over time, Cruz became more than just a student; he became a son. Hooper and Gale, though initially hesitant, eventually adopted him in 1998, giving him the last name Hooper. This decision was not without controversy, as it was uncommon for white individuals to adopt Mexican children during that time. However, Cruz’s transformation from a troubled student to a responsible adult was evident, and he eventually graduated with his peers and went on to attend Texas Tech University.

Today, Cruz, now known as Cruz Hooper, lives in San Antonio with his wife, Anel Montemayor-Hooper, and their two children. He is careful to teach his children about their Mexican heritage while also honoring the Hooper family traditions. Reflecting on his journey, Cruz credits Hooper and Gale for their unwavering support and for helping him find his path. For Hooper, Cruz represents the one thing she has done right in her life, and she is proud of the impact she has had on his life and the lives of her students.
